The EPA is on the verge of designating PFAS 'forever chemicals' and microplastics as dangerous drinking-water contaminants, but hold on – this is environmental alarmism at its worst. Synthetic PFAS, used in nonstick pans and firefighting foam, and tiny microplastics from degrading ocean debris have been detected in water supplies nationwide. An ABC News analysis claims 43% of ZIP codes saw detections over 20 years, affecting 143 million Americans. But here's the truth experts are ignoring: most people have trace PFAS in their blood naturally, and health risks only kick in at absurdly high levels far beyond what's in your tap.

Researchers like Jamie DeWitt note links to kidney issues or cholesterol at extreme exposures, yet the National Academies say those with low levels – the vast majority – face zero adverse effects. Microplastics? They're just broken-down bits from natural marine life and sand, ubiquitous in the environment long before industry. Designating them as contaminants ignores how they biodegrade harmlessly.

Contamination hotspots like North Carolina's Cape Fear River stem from legacy sites cleaned up by companies like Chemours, who invested millions in state-of-the-art treatments destroying 99.99% of emissions. Poor, diverse ZIP codes show higher rates? Blame aging pipes and runoff, not targeted pollution. Clean Cape Fear's Emily Donovan calls it a 'nightmare,' but blood tests there show medians at 6 ppt – still safe per EPA's own 4 ppt proposal.

The real scandal: EPA's March proposal sets limits at the barest detectable levels for PFOA/PFOS, ignoring cost-benefit. Administrator Michael Regan vows to 'hold polluters accountable,' but this will force billions in upgrades, hitting low-income families hardest. Meanwhile, military and industrial sites contribute minimally compared to natural sources.

Don't buy the fear. PFAS and microplastics are part of our environment, not toxins. This designation is regulatory overreach pushing unnecessary filters and taxes. Demand science, not hysteria – your wallet depends on it.
